chronology

/kruh-NOL-uh-jee/ — stress on NOL · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A chronology is the order in which a set of events happened, laid out from earliest to latest.

The museum wall shows a chronology of flight, from balloons to rockets.

Example

A detective interviews five witnesses to a car accident. Each person remembers the events in a different order—some say the traffic light failed first, others say the crash happened before that. She carefully creates a chronology, placing each event in the exact sequence from earliest to latest.

Chronology is more precise than "sequence" or "list" because it specifically names the time-based order of events. In an investigation, getting the chronology right is crucial because cause and effect depend on what happened when—not just any order, but events arranged from earliest to latest.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sequence: A sequence is simply the order in which things follow one another — steps, numbers, moves — with no claim about time or dates. A chronology is a particular kind of sequence: real events arranged by when they happened, from earliest to latest.

timeline: A timeline pins events to their dates along a drawn line of time, so you can see at a glance when each one happened. A chronology needs no picture and no exact dates — it is the earliest-to-latest order of events itself, whether or not anyone draws it.

record: A record is a written account of what has already happened, kept so it is not forgotten — minutes, logs, files. A chronology goes further than keeping: it arranges those happenings by time, from earliest to latest. A record preserves; a chronology orders.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

chaos: complete disorder with no sequence at all

jumble: a confused, unordered mix of things

Where it sits · how strictly events are arranged by time

chaos → jumble → chronology → meticulously documented order

chaos vs. chronology: Chaos is the total opposite end of the scale from chronology: chaos has no order at all, while a chronology arranges every event in its proper place in time.

jumble vs. chronology: A jumble is less disordered than chaos but still far from a chronology — a jumble mixes events up carelessly, while a chronology lines them up from earliest to latest.

meticulously documented order vs. chronology: A meticulously documented order is even stronger than a chronology: a chronology puts events in time order, but a meticulously documented order records every detail of each event with painstaking care.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — chrono-: time (from Greek chronos, 'time'; the final o is the Greek linking vowel)

Suffix — -logy: an account or study of (from Greek logos)

Put it together: Chrono- ('time,' from Greek chronos) + -logy ('an account or study of') literally builds 'an account of time' — exactly what a chronology is: a set of events laid out in the order they happened.

Use the root in a new word: chronic: His chronic cough finally sent him to the doctor after the third week.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / academic

Use chronology in historical, investigative, or analytical contexts where the time-based order of events matters. For a simple list of items without emphasis on time, sequence or list is adequate.
